core.definition: Archaic word for learning or a lesson, now found mainly in old texts and in older English literature.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is short, like the 'i' in 'lit,' followed by a clear r. Don't stretch it into 'leer,' and don't confuse it with 'learn.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in old texts, but a modern speaker using it would sound odd or pretentious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans do not use 'lear' in ordinary speech; they say 'learning,' 'a lesson,' or 'what I learned.' You will meet it in Middle English and early modern texts, and in the name of Shakespeare's King Lear. Do not use it in your own writing or speech.

distinctions.note: Learn is the modern verb for acquiring knowledge; lear is an archaic noun for learning or teaching and is not used today.
A lesson is the common modern noun for something taught or learned, while lear is archaic and mainly literary.

examples.professional: The archival lear in this 1800s manuscript is useful for understanding local teaching practices.
examples.analytical: The medieval lear of the monastery was transmitted through careful copying and commentary.

nuance.analogy: Lear is like an old coin in a museum case: valuable for history, but not something you spend in daily life.
nuance.etymology: From Old English lār, teaching or learning, which is related to the verb learn.
common_mistakes: Using 'lear' as a modern word for learning, which sounds archaic or like a misspelling.
Writing 'lear' as a substitute for 'learn,' which is a misspelling and should be avoided.

lear.etymology: From Middle English *laire*, *leire*, *lere*, northern Middle English variants of *lore*, *loare* (“doctrine, teaching, lore”), from Old English *lār* (“lore”).

senses.definition: A tough material produced from the skin of animals, by tanning or similar process, used e.g. for clothing; often denotes leather from cattle when no qualifier specifies otherwise.
senses.example: The saddle was made of thick brown leather that had been polished by years of use.

senses.definition: A piece of the above used for polishing.
senses.example: She rubbed the silver spoons with a soft leather until they gleamed.

senses.definition: A cricket ball or football.
senses.example: The bowler shone the leather on his trousers before the new over began.

senses.definition: (plural: leathers) clothing made from the skin of animals, often worn by motorcycle riders.
senses.example: He pulled on his leathers, kicked his bike to life, and rode out toward the coast.

senses.definition: A punch.
senses.example: He threw a leather at the bouncer, and the whole bar went silent.

senses.definition: Clipping of fruit leather.
senses.example: We bought a bag of mango leather at the farmers market for the hike.

senses.definition: A good defensive play.
senses.example: Jones showed good leather to snare that liner.

senses.definition: (dated) The skin.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Made of leather.
senses.example: She wore a leather jacket to the interview, which her mother found scandalous.

senses.definition: Referring to one who wears leather clothing (motorcycle jacket, chaps over 501 jeans, boots), especially as a sign of sadomasochistic homosexuality.
senses.example: The bar downtown caters to a leather crowd on Thursday nights.

senses.definition: Referring to an establishment of familial relations through agreed sexual or romantic deviance.
senses.example: They describe their household as a leather family, with clear rules agreed by everyone.

senses.definition: To cover with leather.
senses.example: The carpenter leathered the arm of the chair to match the sofa.

senses.definition: To form a leathery surface (on).
senses.example: Years of sun had leathered his face until it looked like an old saddle.

senses.definition: To strike forcefully.
senses.example: He leathered the ball all the way down the street.

senses.definition: To spank or beat with a leather belt or strap.
senses.example: Their father used to leather the boys with a belt when they lied.

core.definition: A tough, flexible material made from animal skin that has been tanned, used for clothing, shoes, bags and furniture.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The vowel is short, as in 'let', not the long 'ee' of 'leave'. The th is voiced, and the final -er is a reduced, r-colored syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. Leather suggests quality and durability, though cheap imitations can seem less appealing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use leather for the material in everyday shopping, such as a leather wallet or leather couch, and say 'real leather' or 'genuine leather' to contrast with fake products. In the adjective sense, leather can refer to motorcycle clothing and to the leather subculture, which has its own vocabulary, so the word can carry a specific meaning in some circles. In ordinary conversation, use it for the material, not for people.

distinctions.note: A hide is raw, unprocessed animal skin, while leather is hide that has been tanned to make it durable.
Suede is leather finished on the flesh side so it has a soft, napped surface, rather than the smooth grain side.
Vinyl or faux leather is a synthetic imitation; calling something leather implies real animal hide.

examples.everyday: I bought a leather wallet at the mall, and it already smells great.
examples.professional: The procurement team asked us to specify full-grain leather for the new seat covers.
examples.analytical: Historically, leather was valued because tanning turned perishable hide into a durable material that could be shaped and worn.

nuance.analogy: Think of raw hide as dough and leather as bread: tanning transforms a perishable material into something that lasts.
nuance.etymology: From Old English lēðer, of Germanic origin; the deeper root is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Using the long ee vowel from 'leave' instead of the short e in 'leather'.
Treating leather as countable; say 'a piece of leather' or 'a leather jacket', not 'a leather' for the material.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Scriptures, the word 'ôr refers to skin or hide, and tanned hides were used for tent coverings and sacred furnishings, as in Exodus 25:5 in the Revised Standard Version. In the New Testament, the Greek dermatinē describes John the Baptist's leather girdle in Mark 1:6, a sign of his simple, rough life in the wilderness. Acts 9:43 mentions Simon the tanner in Joppa, showing that tanning was a respected trade in the early church's world.

leather.etymology: From Middle English *lether*, from Old English *leþer* (“leather”), from **leþr*, from Proto-Germanic **leþrą* (“leather”), possibly borrowed from **ɸlitrom*, **letros*, from Proto-Indo-European **pel-* (“skin, hide”).

senses.definition: To disappoint; to betray or fail somebody.
senses.example: I promised him I would meet him there, and I will not let him down.

senses.definition: To lengthen by undoing and resewing a hem.
senses.example: She let down the hem of my wool trousers so they fit properly.

senses.definition: To reduce one's level of effort.
senses.example: Coach told us never to let down during the second half, even when ahead.

senses.definition: To soften in tempering.
senses.example: to let down tools or cutlery

senses.definition: To thin; to reduce the thickness or viscosity of.
senses.example: let the sauce down with a little pasta water if it starts to become too thick; if the soup is too thick, you can let it down with a little milk; let the sauce down with a dash of the pickling liquor; use some of the stock to let down the onion sauce

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see let,‎ down: especially, to allow to descend.
senses.example: let down your hair

core.definition: To disappoint someone by failing to do what they expected or trusted you to do.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'down'. 'Let' is short and light, and the final t in 'let' is often barely released before 'down'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies that you broke someone's trust or expectations, so it can hurt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it constantly with people, as in 'I don't want to let you down'. It is more personal than 'disappoint', which can describe disappointing news or results. Shifting the object between 'let down' and 'let [someone] down' is standard, but the object must come between 'let' and 'down' when it is a pronoun, as in 'let me down'.

distinctions.note: 'Disappoint' is more general and neutral, and can describe things as well as people. 'Let down' focuses on failing someone who relied on you.
'Fail' describes not meeting a standard or goal. 'Let down' emphasizes the person who was counting on you.

examples.everyday: Sorry I missed your birthday dinner, I didn't mean to let you down.
examples.professional: We can't let the client down on the Friday deadline, so I'm moving two tasks to tomorrow.
examples.analytical: The model's failure on rare cases let down its early promise, and the authors had to revise their claims.

nuance.analogy: Like a ladder that gives way when you step on it: the support you counted on suddenly fails.
nuance.etymology: From 'let' (allow, release) plus 'down'; the sense of lowering or dropping developed into failing someone.
common_mistakes: Writing 'let down' as one word in a verb phrase; the noun 'letdown' is one word, but the verb is two.
Using it for things that didn't work well; 'disappointing' or 'a failure' is often better for objects.

conversation.text: I promised I'd come, and I don't want to let you down.
After all the hype, the movie really let me down.
Let the rope down slowly so the bucket doesn't spill.
I felt really let down when he didn't show up.
Sorry I let you down. I'll do better next time.

senses.definition: An identifying tag, usually made of metal, bearing a sequence of letters or numbers identifying the vehicle, and placed at the rear and, often, also at the front of a motor vehicle.
senses.example: The police officer wrote down the car's license plate number after the minor collision.

core.definition: A metal or plastic tag attached to a vehicle, usually at the front and rear, displaying the vehicle's registration letters and numbers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAI in 'license' and on the second word, 'plate', with a weaker secondary stress. The 'se' sound in license is reduced to 'sun'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'license plate' every day for the tag on a car, and it is the standard term across the country. In British English this is called a 'number plate,' so do not use that phrase in the United States. People also talk about a 'vanity plate' for a personalized one.

distinctions.note: Number plate is the British term for the same object, while Americans use license plate.
The license plate is the physical tag on the car, while the registration is the official document that goes with it.

examples.everyday: I think I saw your license plate in the parking lot, so your car is probably still here.
examples.professional: The parking app matches each visitor's license plate number to a pass before the gate opens.
examples.analytical: Automated license plate readers raise questions about privacy, because they record vehicle locations at scale.

nuance.analogy: A license plate is like a name tag on a car, letting anyone identify it quickly.
nuance.etymology: License comes from Latin licentia, meaning permission; plate comes from Old French plate, meaning a flat piece of metal.
common_mistakes: Saying 'number plate' in the United States, which sounds British.
Stressing 'PLATE' too strongly; the primary stress stays on LAI.

conversation.text: I didn't get his license plate number before he drove off.
Her license plate says "BKWORM," so she's obviously a big reader.
When you move to a new state, you have to get new license plates.

senses.definition: Blood that is needed for continued life; blood regarded as the seat of life.
senses.example: The surgeon worried about how much lifeblood the patient had lost before the ambulance arrived.

senses.definition: That which is required for continued existence or function.
senses.example: Gasoline is the lifeblood of the modern city.

core.definition: The thing that is most essential to the survival, success, or vitality of something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LIFE on the first syllable and keep the blood vowel short and relaxed, like the u in 'mud'. The final d is clear, so avoid saying 'blood' with a long oo sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It describes something vital and indispensable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lifeblood figuratively for something a business, community, or relationship cannot survive without: 'Customers are the lifeblood of this store.' The literal sense of blood as life is more common in religious or literary writing. The word sounds a bit dramatic, so it works best in speeches, articles, or descriptions rather than casual remarks.

distinctions.note: A lifeline is a means of rescue or support in a crisis, while lifeblood is what sustains something continuously.
Backbone is the core strength or foundation of something, while lifeblood stresses that it is essential for ongoing life.

examples.everyday: Coffee is the lifeblood of this office, especially on Monday mornings.
examples.professional: Recurring revenue is the lifeblood of our subscription business, so retention is our top priority.
examples.analytical: For Leviticus, blood is the lifeblood of the body, a sign that life belongs to God and must not be eaten.

nuance.analogy: Like the blood moving through a body: when it flows well, everything works; when it stops, the whole system weakens.
nuance.etymology: Compound of life and blood, from Old English līf and blōd.
common_mistakes: Writing 'life blood' as two words in American English; the standard form is one word.
Using it for ordinary minor help; it implies something essential, not just useful.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew, the key words are nephesh (נֶפֶשׁ), meaning life or soul, and dam (דָּם), meaning blood. Leviticus 17:11 says that the life of the flesh is in the blood, and Deuteronomy 12:23 says that the blood is the life. These passages forbid eating blood because it belongs to God as the giver of life and is used in atonement.

senses.definition: A predetermined or prescribed set of rituals that are performed, usually by a religion; a book in which they are recorded.
senses.example: The congregation followed the liturgy printed in the bulletin, reciting each response together.

senses.definition: An official worship service of the Christian church.
senses.example: Our parish celebrates a sung liturgy every Sunday morning at nine o'clock.

senses.definition: (historical) In Ancient Greece, a form of personal service to the state.
senses.example: In classical Athens, the richest citizens were expected to perform a liturgy by financing a warship.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The prescribed form of public worship in a church, including its prayers, readings, and actions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: LIT-ur-jee. The t is a flap, so it sounds close to d, and the g is j.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; can sound reverent or rigid depending on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, 'the Divine Liturgy' is the Orthodox Eucharistic service, and Catholics speak of the Liturgy of the Word and Eucharist. It is also used loosely for any repeated routine, as in 'the liturgy of morning rituals'.

distinctions.note: Service is the general word for a worship gathering, while liturgy implies a fixed, structured order.
Ritual can be any repeated ceremonial act, while liturgy is the formal public worship of a church.
Mass is the Catholic Eucharistic celebration, one specific liturgy among many.

examples.everyday: We go to the Divine Liturgy every Sunday morning at nine.
examples.professional: The seminary offers a course on the history and theology of Christian liturgy.
examples.analytical: The liturgy is not merely a form of worship but a way the Church teaches and embodies its faith.

nuance.analogy: Liturgy is like a shared script through which a whole community prays in unison.
nuance.etymology: From Greek leitourgia, public service, from laos (people) and ergon (work).
common_mistakes: Saying 'LIE-ter-jee' with a long i.
Using it to mean any sermon or church event.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek leitourgia means service, and the verb leitourgeo appears in Acts 13:2, where the church at Antioch was worshiping the Lord. Luke 1:23 uses it for Zechariah's priestly service in the temple. Hebrews 8:6 speaks of Christ's ministry (leitourgia) as superior to the old one.

traditions.view: The Divine Liturgy is the central act of worship, a participation in heavenly worship, normally using the liturgies of St. John Chrysostom or St. Basil.
The liturgy, especially the Mass, is the public worship of the Church and 'the source and summit' of Christian life, governed by approved texts.
Lutherans and Anglicans keep ordered liturgies. Reformed churches use simpler forms, and Baptist and Pentecostal churches often prefer free-form worship, though they still have an order of service.

liturgy.etymology: From Middle French *liturgie*, from Latin *liturgia*, from Ancient Greek *λειτουργία*, from *λειτ-*, from *λαός* (“people”) + *-ουργός*, from *ἔργον* (“work”).

senses.definition: The state or quality of being livid.
senses.example: Her lividity during the meeting was obvious; she was furious at the budget cuts.

senses.definition: A livid area of skin, such as a bruise, or as is often found on cadavers.
senses.example: The forensic report described the lividity along his back, a purplish area from pooled blood.

senses.definition: Livor mortis, suggillation.

core.definition: A purplish or reddish discoloration of skin caused by blood pooling in the body after death, also called livor mortis.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VID. The final syllables are unstressed, with a schwa in the third syllable and a flapped t that sounds like a soft 'd'. Don't say 'lih-VID-it-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical, used in forensic or medical contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use lividity mainly in forensic science, pathology and crime shows to describe the discoloration after death. For anger, Americans use the adjective 'livid', not the noun 'lividity'. In casual conversation the word is rare, and people usually say 'bruising' or 'discoloration'. The Latin term 'livor mortis' is used in medical textbooks.

distinctions.note: Livid is an adjective meaning furiously angry or bruised in color, while lividity is a noun for the forensic discoloration.
A bruise comes from an injury to a living body, while lividity comes from blood settling after death.
Livor mortis is the Latin technical term, used in medical writing, while lividity is the English term.

examples.everyday: The detective explained that the purple marks on his arms were lividity, not bruises.
examples.professional: The medical examiner's report documents fixed lividity on the back, which suggests the body stayed in one position after death.
examples.analytical: Fixed lividity, which appears once blood settles and stops shifting, is one reason forensic scientists can estimate whether a body was moved.

nuance.analogy: Lividity is like wine settling in the bottom of a glass, with the blood pooling in the lowest parts of the body.
nuance.etymology: From Latin lividus, meaning bluish, via the English livid; the noun is formed from the same root.
common_mistakes: Using 'lividity' to describe anger; the anger sense is the adjective 'livid'.
Pronouncing the middle syllables with full vowels, such as 'lih-VID-i-tee', rather than the reduced American form.

lividity.etymology: From Middle English *lividite,lyvydite*, from Middle French *lividité* and its etymon Medieval Latin *līviditās*, from Latin *līvidus* (“livid”) + *-tās*.

senses.definition: To a great height.
With affectation of grandness.
senses.example: She spoke loftily about her summer in Paris, as if the city had been built for her.

core.definition: In a proud, superior manner that looks down on others, or at a great height.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The ending '-ily' is pronounced 'uh-lee' with a reduced middle vowel, not 'ill-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative, since it describes a haughty or condescending manner. The literal 'high up' sense is neutral but rare.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'loftily' in everyday speech. It appears mostly in writing to describe a condescending tone, such as 'She loftily dismissed my question.' For physical height, people say 'high up' or 'high above' instead.

distinctions.note: Both suggest arrogance, but 'haughtily' directly describes proud behavior, while 'loftily' suggests a speaker acting as though above others.
'Proudly' can be positive, meaning with satisfaction, whereas 'loftily' always carries a note of superiority or disdain.

examples.everyday: He answered my question loftily, as if I should have known the answer already.
examples.professional: The vendor responded loftily to our concerns, promising results without any data to back them up.
examples.analytical: The author writes loftily about virtue, yet his argument rests on assumptions he never examines.

nuance.analogy: Speaking loftily is like talking from a balcony while everyone else stands in the street.
nuance.etymology: From 'lofty' (from 'loft', meaning height) plus the adverbial suffix '-ly'.
common_mistakes: Using 'loftily' to mean simply 'high up' in everyday speech; it sounds literary or sarcastic.
Spelling it 'loftly'; the adverb keeps the 'i' and becomes 'loftily'.

senses.definition: The act of making something looser.

core.definition: The act of making something looser, less tight, firm, or restrictive, such as a bolt, a belt, or a rule.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the 'oo' is the long vowel of 'boot'. The second syllable is reduced to a light 'uh', and the '-en' ending is often a syllabic n, so it sounds like 'LOO-suh-ning' with no separate 'eh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a physical or abstract change without judgment, though it can be positive when easing a restriction and negative when weakening a structure.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'loosening' most often for physical fasteners ('the loosening of the lug nuts') and for rules or policies ('a loosening of lending standards'). In everyday speech people more often say 'loosen up' or 'getting looser', so 'loosening' sounds slightly technical or written.

distinctions.note: Relaxation refers to a feeling of calm or rest in a person, while loosening refers to a change in the tightness or strictness of a thing.
Deregulation is a specific political or legal removal of government rules, while loosening is a broader, more general reduction in tightness or strictness.

examples.everyday: The jar lid needs a little loosening before I can get it open.
examples.professional: The loosening of the approval rules let the team ship changes without a second review.
examples.analytical: Historians often trace the loosening of social norms to the rapid growth of cities in the nineteenth century.

nuance.analogy: Like a guitar string being turned down: the tension drops, and the sound changes.
nuance.etymology: From loosen (to make loose) plus the -ing suffix, from Old English lēos, loose.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 's' as a 'z' (it is /s/ in 'loosen', as in 'loose').
Using 'loosening' as a verb instead of the noun; the verb is 'loosen'.

senses.definition: The state or property of being lopsided.

core.definition: The quality of being uneven or unbalanced, with one side heavier, larger, or more favored than the other.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-ness' is a weak, unstressed 'nus' with a reduced vowel, and the middle 'sided' is a quick 'sy-did'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral. It names a flaw or imbalance and often appears in analysis or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'lopsidedness' mainly in analysis, criticism, or formal writing about trade, budgets, votes, or design. In casual speech people say 'it's lopsided' or 'it's unfair' instead. It is a precise, somewhat formal noun, so it sounds natural in reports and essays.

distinctions.note: Imbalance is a broader, more neutral word that can describe economic, mental, or physical situations, while lopsidedness emphasizes an uneven shape or distribution.
Asymmetry is a precise term for lack of symmetry, often used neutrally in science or design, while lopsidedness often implies a flaw.

collocations: the lopsidedness of the tax code
the lopsidedness of the trade deal

examples.everyday: I noticed the lopsidedness of the sofa once I put the heavy pillows on one end.
examples.professional: The report highlighted the lopsidedness of our hiring pipeline, which was overwhelmingly from one university.
examples.analytical: The lopsidedness of the constitutional arrangement made it hard for smaller states to influence national policy.

nuance.analogy: Like a seesaw with one child on one end and nobody on the other, the whole thing tips toward the heavy side.
nuance.etymology: From lopsided plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using 'lopsidedness' as a verb or adjective; it is only a noun.
Spelling it with a 'u' in the middle or dropping the final 'ness'.

senses.definition: The bags and other containers that hold a traveler's belongings.
The contents of such containers.
senses.example: Airport security asked him to unpack all of the luggage for inspection.

core.definition: The suitcases, bags and other containers that hold a traveler's belongings, especially during a trip.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and say the final syllable as a reduced 'ij' sound, not 'ayj'. The g is hard, as in 'bug'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: It is practical and describes objects rather than feelings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans treat luggage as an uncountable noun for all bags together, so say 'my luggage' or 'a piece of luggage,' not 'a luggage.' For one bag, say suitcase, carry-on or duffel bag. At airports Americans also say baggage, as in 'checked baggage,' and a common reply to 'Do you have any checked bags?' is 'Just this carry-on.'

distinctions.note: Baggage is the common American term in airline and airport contexts, and it also has a figurative sense for emotional history, while luggage is the everyday word for bags you travel with.
A suitcase is one specific piece of luggage, while luggage is the general word for all of them together.

examples.everyday: Can you help me get my luggage down from the overhead bin?
examples.professional: The airline lost our team's luggage, so we are having the equipment shipped to the hotel tomorrow.
examples.analytical: A traveler's luggage often reveals more about their plans than their conversation does.

nuance.analogy: Like a backpack for an entire trip: everything you bring along, gathered in one place.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain, perhaps from lug (to haul) with the suffix -age, though the link is not certain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'luggages' or 'a luggage,' since luggage is uncountable in American English.
Using luggage for a single bag, where suitcase or bag is correct.

luggage.etymology: 1590s, *lug* + *age*, literally “that which is lugged, dragged around”.

senses.definition: In a lugubrious manner.

core.definition: In a mournful, gloomy or exaggeratedly sad manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the GOO syllable, then reduce the -ous to 'us' and end with '-lee'. The r in 'bree' is clear in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative, suggesting exaggerated or performed gloom. It can be playful when describing someone's behavior.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb appears in written descriptions of how someone speaks, moves, or sighs. Americans rarely use it in conversation. A more natural spoken option is 'with a long face' or 'sadly'.

distinctions.note: Sadly is neutral and common, while lugubriously describes an exaggerated, theatrical sadness.
Mournfully focuses on grief, while lugubriously suggests a gloomy display that may seem excessive.

examples.everyday: He sat on the porch and sighed lugubriously every time someone mentioned the Mets.
examples.professional: The manager read the forecast lugubriously, which made the sales team assume the worst before she had finished.
examples.analytical: The narrator recounts his failures lugubriously, inviting the reader to pity him while also doubting his sincerity.

nuance.analogy: Like a weather report delivered in a funeral voice: the delivery is heavier than the news.
nuance.etymology: From lugubrious, from Latin lugubris, from lugere 'to mourn'.
common_mistakes: Using it for ordinary sadness in casual conversation, where 'sadly' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables as 'loo-goo-BREE-us-lee'.

senses.definition: A person who lunges.
A person afflicted with a disease of the lungs, especially one suffering from tuberculosis.
senses.example: The sanatorium was full of lungers who came to the mountains to breathe clean air.

senses.definition: A vehicle whose engine has the specified number of cylinders.
senses.example: Our old pickup is a four-lunger, so it drinks gas but climbs hills well.

core.definition: A person who lunges, especially one who works a horse on a long line in training.

pronunciation.tip: The 'ng' is a single nasal sound, with no 'g' after it. The final syllable is an American 'r-colored' 'er,' not 'ar' or 'or.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and specialized. In horse training it is a neutral job title, and the older sense about lung disease sounds dated.
nuance.usage_note: Most Americans will not use 'lunger' in everyday talk. In horse training it refers to the handler who directs the horse on a lunge line; equestrians may say 'the lunger' or 'longeing' instead. The older sense, a person with tuberculosis, is archaic and should be avoided today.

distinctions.note: Lunge is the action of moving forward suddenly; lunger is the person who performs the lunging or handling.
A lunge line is the long rope used in training; a lunger is the person holding it.

examples.professional: Our equine program needs another certified lunger for the Tuesday training sessions.
examples.analytical: The lunger's role is often described as a technical craft, not a mere helper, because the handler controls the horse's balance and rhythm.

nuance.analogy: A lunger is like the person holding the center of a spinning tether, keeping the horse moving in a steady circle.
nuance.etymology: Formed from 'lunge' with the agent suffix '-er.' The older lung-disease sense is a separate use related to 'lung.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'lunger' with 'lunge' (the action) or with 'lung' (the organ).
Using the archaic tuberculosis sense in modern conversation.
Pronouncing the 'ng' with a hard 'g' sound.

senses.definition: Very fine in quality and comfortable.
senses.example: a luxurious hotel suite

senses.definition: (dated) Enjoying the pleasures of luxury, accustomed to luxury.
senses.example: The wealthy widow lived a luxurious life, attended by servants and fine silks.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Very expensive, comfortable and high quality, providing great pleasure and comfort.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the middle syllable, -ZHUR-. The ending -ous is reduced to 'uhs', and the first syllable is weak.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests comfort, quality and pleasure, though it can sound excessive when used for things that are unnecessary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use luxurious for hotels, cars, fabrics, food and lifestyles. It is common in advertising, travel talk and shopping. In casual speech people might say fancy or upscale, but luxurious is perfectly natural and widely used.

distinctions.note: Expensive refers only to high cost, while luxurious adds the idea of comfort and pleasure.
Lavish suggests generous or extravagant spending, often in a large or showy way, while luxurious emphasizes comfort and quality.
Opulent is more formal and suggests grand, rich display, often with gold or elaborate decoration.

examples.everyday: We stayed at a luxurious hotel near the beach, and the bed was amazing.
examples.professional: The client wants a luxurious feel for the new lobby, but the budget is limited.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that a luxurious lifestyle can disguise social inequality behind the pleasures of comfort.

nuance.analogy: A luxurious room is like a warm wool coat in winter: soft, expensive and very comfortable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin luxuria, meaning excess, through Old French luxurios.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'luck-shur-ee-us' with a hard k; the American sound is closer to 'lug-ZHUR-ee-us'.
Using luxurious for the noun luxury, as in 'a luxurious of cars'; say 'a luxury car'.

luxurious.etymology: From Middle English *luxurious*, from Old French *luxurios*, from Latin *lū̆xuriōsus* (“rank, luxuriant, profuse, excessive, immoderate”), from *lū̆xuria* (“rankness, luxury”), from *lū̆xus* (“extravagance, luxury”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to Macarius of Egypt, Egyptian Christian monk and hermit.

core.definition: Relating to Macarius of Egypt, a fourth-century Christian monk, or to the spiritual writings attributed to him, especially the Macarian Homilies on prayer and inner experience.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the second syllable 'KAIR', and the 'ar' is pronounced as in 'air' with a rhotic r. The final syllable is reduced to 'un'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in academic writing on early Christian monasticism, Orthodox spirituality or patristic studies. It is rarely heard in everyday speech. In a seminary or theology class you might hear it when discussing the Macarian Homilies.

distinctions.note: Macarene is not a standard English word; Macarian is the correct adjective for Macarius of Egypt or related writings.
Macedonian refers to Macedonia, the region in the Greek and Roman world or the modern country, and is unrelated to the monk Macarius.

examples.professional: In the reading list for our patristics seminar, the Macarian material is listed under the desert fathers.
examples.analytical: The Macarian corpus presents the heart as the seat of prayer, a theme that later Orthodox mystics developed in their accounts of inner stillness.

nuance.analogy: Like a window onto the desert monks of Egypt, where the inner life is the real landscape.
nuance.etymology: From Macarius, the Latinized form of the Greek name Makarios, meaning 'blessed' or 'happy'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'MAK-uh-ree-un'.
Confusing Macarian with Macedonian, which refers to a different place and people.

senses.definition: A gang elder in prison.
senses.example: Nobody in the cell block crossed the maestro, because his word settled every dispute between the gangs.

senses.definition: A master in some art, especially a composer or conductor.

core.definition: A highly skilled master of an art, especially a celebrated orchestra conductor or composer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, pronounced like the word 'my'. Do not use the Italian mah-EH-stroh; in American speech the t is clearly pronounced before the r, and the final vowel is a long oh.

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring; it praises skill, and it can be playful or ironic when used for someone who excels at an everyday task like cooking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use maestro mainly for famous conductors and composers, and as a friendly compliment for someone who excels at something, like grilling. Calling a non-Italian conductor maestro is normal in American concert reviews. The prison slang sense, a gang elder, is rare and specialized, so avoid it in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Master is a general word for an expert or teacher; maestro implies artistic brilliance and public admiration.
A virtuoso is a performer with exceptional technique; a maestro is often a conductor or composer who shapes and leads the whole work.

examples.everyday: My dad is a total maestro at the grill, and he always knows exactly when the steaks are done.
examples.professional: The company hired a maestro of project management who could keep five teams moving in the same direction.
examples.analytical: Schenker treated the analyst as a kind of maestro whose hearing of structural unity came from long, disciplined practice rather than intuition alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a head chef leading a busy kitchen: the maestro sets the tempo, balances the parts and gets the best from every player.
nuance.etymology: From Italian maestro, master, from Latin magister.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it the Italian way, mah-EH-stroh; Americans say MY-stroh.
Using it as a general word for any teacher or boss, which sounds exaggerated.

senses.definition: A literary style or genre that combines naturalistic details and narrative with surreal or dreamlike elements.
senses.example: Her novel uses magical realism, with a grandmother who floats above her bed during the storm.

core.definition: A literary style that blends realistic, everyday detail with dreamlike or supernatural events presented as ordinary.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the word REAL and the word ISM, with the stronger stress on REE. Link the words and say 'MAJ-ih-kul REE-uh-liz-um' fluidly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a respected term in literary criticism that describes a style.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in literature classes, book clubs, and literary reviews, often when discussing Latin American writers such as Gabriel García Márquez. In everyday conversation it is rarely used. If someone describes a novel as 'magical realism', they mean the magic is treated as ordinary, not as a fantasy with rules.

distinctions.note: Fantasy usually builds a separate magical world, while magical realism places magic in an ordinary, realistic setting.
Surrealism is a movement in art and literature that seeks dream logic, while magical realism keeps a realistic tone and detail.

examples.everyday: My book club is reading a novel with magical realism, where the ghosts are just part of everyday life.
examples.professional: The marketing copy calls the film magical realism, which helped it find an audience of literary readers.
examples.analytical: Magical realism challenges the boundary between the natural and the supernatural, forcing readers to accept both as part of the same reality.

nuance.analogy: Magical realism is like a photograph taken in a familiar kitchen where, on one shelf, a jar is quietly glowing and no one remarks on it.
nuance.etymology: Coined in German as magischer Realismus by art critic Franz Roh in 1925, and later popularized in Latin American literature.
common_mistakes: Using 'magical realism' to mean any fantasy novel, which is inaccurate.
Stressing 'MAJ-ih-kul' and 'ree-AL-izm' with the wrong stress on the second word.

senses.definition: One who creates works in the style of magic realism.

core.definition: A writer or artist who creates works in magic realism, which mixes realistic detail with magical or fantastic events.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on REE in realist, and magical has a lighter secondary stress on MAJ. Keep the r clear in both words, and say realist as REE-uh-list, not REAL-ist.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it praises a writer's imaginative style, though it can sound vague if used loosely.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term in literature classes, book reviews and book clubs, often for Latin American writers such as Gabriel García Márquez and Isabel Allende. In conversation, you might say 'She's a magical realist, so the book has ghosts and everyday details side by side.' Some writers reject the label, so be careful when describing a particular author.

distinctions.note: Magic realism is the style or movement; a magical realist is the person who writes or paints in it.
A fabulist tells fables or invented stories with a moral; a magical realist keeps everyday realistic detail alongside the fantastic.
A science fiction writer explains fantastic events through imagined science; a magical realist usually leaves the fantastic unexplained.

examples.everyday: My book club is reading a magical realist novel this month, so I'm trying to keep up with the ghosts and the family drama.
examples.professional: The editor asked me to pitch the book to the marketing team as a magical realist story, which helped them understand its tone.
examples.analytical: As a magical realist, Márquez treats the miraculous with the same plain tone as the mundane, which makes the fantastic feel ordinary and political.

nuance.analogy: A magical realist is like a painter who depicts a dreamlike scene with the careful detail of a photograph.
nuance.etymology: From magical plus realist. The term magic realism came from German magischer Realismus, coined by the art critic Franz Roh in 1925.
common_mistakes: Confusing magical realist, the writer, with magic realism, the style; say magic realism for the movement.
Pronouncing realist with a long a, as in REAL-ist; say REE-uh-list.

senses.definition: The quality of being impressive, great, dignified, powerful, sovereign, or any combination thereof.
senses.example: the majesty of the Great Pyramids

core.definition: A quality of grandeur, dignity, and power that commands awe, especially in nature, in a ruler, or in God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MAJ. The second syllable is weak and reduced to 'uh,' so avoid saying 'ma-JES-tee,' which is a common error.

nuance.connotation: Positive and elevated. It implies greatness and dignity, and it is used for royalty, nature, and the sacred.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use 'Your Majesty' or 'Her Majesty' when addressing or referring to a monarch, a usage they encounter mainly in film, news, and literature. In ordinary speech they more often say 'grandeur' or 'beauty' about nature. Using 'majesty' for everyday things can sound ironic or overdone.

distinctions.note: Grandeur emphasizes impressive size or splendor, while majesty adds a sense of dignity, authority, or sovereignty.
Dignity refers to calm self-respect or worth, which can be personal, while majesty is more about commanding presence or royal and divine authority.

examples.everyday: Standing on the rim of the Grand Canyon, we were struck by the majesty of the view.
examples.professional: The brand guide asks us to capture the majesty of the product without making it feel exclusive.
examples.analytical: The psalmist speaks of God as clothed in majesty, and this image shapes how the whole creation is read as a sign of divine rule.

nuance.analogy: Majesty is like a cathedral's height and light: it fills the space with a sense of greatness that makes you lower your voice.
nuance.etymology: From Latin maiestas, 'greatness,' from maior, 'greater.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (ma-JES-ty) instead of the first (MAJ-uh-stee).
Pronouncing the ending as 'mah-jess-tee' with full vowels.
Using 'majesty' as a title without 'Your' or 'Her' before it, which sounds unnatural in English.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, majesty describes the splendor and kingly dignity of God and of God's reign. The Hebrew words hod and gaon convey glory, honor, and majesty, and in Greek the New Testament uses megaleiotes and megalosyne for divine majesty. Psalm 93:1 describes the LORD as robed in majesty and reigning as king. Hebrews 1:3 speaks of the Son sitting at the right hand of the Majesty on high. 2 Peter 1:16 says the apostles were eyewitnesses of Christ's majesty at the transfiguration.

majesty.etymology: From Middle English *majeste*, *mageste*, from Old French *majesté*, from Latin *maiestas*,

senses.definition: To repair a relationship; to resolve an argument or fight; to make reparations or redress.
senses.example: I hope they can stop fighting and make amends.

core.definition: To repair harm you caused, by apologizing, paying back, or doing something that restores a damaged relationship.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'mends', the second syllable of 'amends'. The final 'z' sound in 'amends' is voiced, like 'ends'. Do not say 'a-MENDS' with a long vowel in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive and serious. It suggests moral responsibility and a sincere effort to repair damage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in serious personal or professional situations: after a fight with a friend, a business error or a legal settlement. In everyday speech, it sounds more sincere and careful than 'sorry' alone. It is usually followed by 'for' (make amends for something) or 'with' (make amends with someone).

distinctions.note: 'Apologize' expresses regret in words; 'make amends' includes repairing or compensating for the harm.
'Make up for' is more everyday and can be lighter; 'make amends' suggests a more serious wrong and an intentional effort to repair it.

examples.everyday: I forgot your birthday, so let me take you to dinner to make amends.
examples.professional: After the outage, the team worked late to make amends with the clients who lost data.
examples.analytical: Many ethicists argue that to make amends for a wrong, one must do more than express regret; one must repair the harm.

nuance.analogy: Like rebuilding a fence you knocked down, the goal is to restore what was damaged, not just to say you are sorry.
nuance.etymology: 'Amends' comes from Old French amender, from Latin emendare, meaning to correct.
common_mistakes: Using the singular 'make amend'; the idiom is almost always plural, 'make amends'.
Using 'make amends' for a trivial action; it is usually for real harm or hurt.

senses.definition: Not adroit; awkward, clumsy, inept.
Somebody who is inept, or lacking in skill, or talent.
senses.example: He was a maladroit at everything, from carpentry to cooking.

core.definition: Clumsy or awkward in a way that shows a lack of skill or tact, especially in dealing with people or delicate situations.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DROYT, the last syllable. The first syllable is 'mal' as in 'mall,' and the middle syllable reduces to 'uh.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes clumsy or tactless behavior, often with a hint of polite disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. It appears mainly in writing, editorials, or literary criticism. In everyday speech, 'clumsy,' 'awkward,' or 'tactless' would be more natural.

distinctions.note: 'Clumsy' refers to physical awkwardness, while 'maladroit' can describe social or verbal tactlessness too.
'Inept' suggests a general lack of competence, while 'maladroit' emphasizes awkwardness in handling a particular situation.

examples.everyday: That was a maladroit joke at the wedding, and his brother was not amused.
examples.professional: The manager's maladroit handling of the layoffs damaged trust across the whole department.
examples.analytical: The author's maladroit metaphors weaken an otherwise careful argument about moral responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Like someone trying to thread a needle while wearing thick gloves, a maladroit person struggles with a task that calls for finesse.
nuance.etymology: From French maladroit, from mal (badly) plus adroit (skillful).
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as 'maladroit' with a stressed 'mal,' or confusing its spelling with 'malodorous.'
Using it as a noun in everyday speech; the noun 'maladroit' is rare and mainly literary.

core.definition: An older English spelling of Manasseh, used in some Bibles, including the King James Version, for the same son of Joseph or the same king of Judah.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NASS. The final -es is pronounced eez, not ez, and the first vowel is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the spelling sounds old-fashioned to modern readers.
nuance.usage_note: You will mainly meet this spelling in older Bibles, quotations and traditional hymns. Modern translations, including the Revised Standard Version, use Manasseh, so use that spelling in study and writing.

distinctions.note: The two names refer to the same person or tribe; Manasseh is the standard modern spelling.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's old Bible spells it Manasses, not Manasseh.
examples.professional: The quotations come from an older translation that spells it Manasses, so I changed the spelling to Manasseh on the slides.
examples.analytical: The spelling Manasses in Matthew 1:10 reflects the Greek form Manasses, which names King Manasseh of Judah in the genealogy of Jesus.

nuance.analogy: Like an old photograph of a familiar face, the spelling is the same person in an older style.
common_mistakes: Using Manasses in modern writing without a reason; readers today expect Manasseh.
Pronouncing the final syllable as ez instead of eez.
nuance.biblical_note: Manasses is an older English spelling used for the same Hebrew name Menasheh. Key passages: Matthew 1:10 (in the genealogy of Jesus, where the Greek form names King Manasseh of Judah); 2 Chronicles 33:10-13 (King Manasseh is taken captive and afterward turns back to God); 2 Kings 21:1 (his long and idolatrous reign is described).

senses.definition: A piece of clothing somewhat like an open robe or cloak, especially that worn by Orthodox bishops.
senses.example: The Orthodox bishop wore a black mantle over his robes during the Easter liturgy.

senses.definition: A figurative garment representing authority or status, capable of affording protection.
senses.example: At the meeting, she finally assumed the mantle of leadership of the party.

senses.definition: Anything that covers or conceals something else; a cloak.
senses.example: A thick mantle of fog covered the valley until almost noon.

senses.definition: The body wall of a mollusc, from which the shell is secreted.
senses.example: The clam's mantle secretes the calcium that builds up its hard shell.

senses.definition: The zone of hot gases around a flame.
senses.example: The hottest part of the candle flame is the outer mantle, where gases burn fully.

senses.definition: A gauzy fabric impregnated with metal nitrates, used in some kinds of gas and oil lamps and lanterns, which forms a rigid but fragile mesh of metal oxides when heated during initial use and then produces white light from the heat of the flame below it.
senses.example: Before we went camping, I replaced the cracked mantle on our old Coleman lantern.

senses.definition: The outer wall and casing of a blast furnace, above the hearth.
senses.example: Engineers inspected the steel mantle of the blast furnace for cracks after the repair.

senses.definition: A penstock for a water wheel.
senses.example: Water rushed through the wooden mantle and turned the old mill wheel with great force.

senses.definition: Any similar layer in an exoplanet.
senses.example: Astronomers modeled the exoplanet's mantle as a thick layer of silicate rock.

senses.definition: The back of a bird together with the folded wings.
senses.example: The robin's mantle was dark gray, and its wings were folded tightly against its back.

senses.definition: The cerebral cortex.
senses.example: Damage to the mantle of the brain can affect memory and language.

senses.definition: The layer between Earth's core and crust.
senses.example: Geologists study how heat rises through the mantle beneath the Earth's crust.

senses.definition: A mantling.
To cover or conceal (something); to cloak; to disguise.
senses.example: Clouds mantled the mountain peaks, so we could not see the summit all day.

senses.definition: To become covered or concealed. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: As the storm approached, the sky mantled slowly with dark gray clouds.

senses.definition: To spread like a mantle (especially of blood in the face and cheeks when a person flushes).
senses.example: Her cheeks mantled with color when the professor praised her research.

senses.definition: To climb over or onto something.
senses.example: The old cat mantled over the fence and dropped into the neighbor's yard.

senses.definition: The action of stretching out the wings to hide food.
senses.example: The hawk mantled over its kill, spreading its wings to shield the meat from rivals.

senses.definition: The action of stretching a wing and the same side leg out to one side of the body.

core.definition: A loose cloak or robe; also a symbol of authority or responsibility passed on to a successor, as in taking up the mantle.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle t is usually a quick flap or soft d, and the final -le is a syllabic l with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It carries weight and dignity and is often used of inherited responsibility.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mantle mostly in figurative phrases such as take up the mantle or the mantle of leadership, often in news, speeches, and sermons. The literal garment appears in religious and historical writing. In casual talk, say take over or take on the role instead.

distinctions.note: A cloak is a practical garment worn outdoors, while a mantle can be literal or figurative and often signals status or authority.
A cape is shorter and covers only the shoulders, while a mantle is usually longer and more formal.

examples.everyday: After Dad retired, my older brother took up the mantle of running the family barbecue.
examples.professional: When our lead engineer left, Maria took up the mantle of owning the deployment pipeline.
examples.analytical: The prophet's mantle in 2 Kings signifies an authority that passes from one generation to the next.

nuance.analogy: Like a coat handed down through a family, the mantle carries the dignity of those who wore it before.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mantellum, 'cloak'.
common_mistakes: Confusing mantle with mantel, the shelf above a fireplace, which is spelled differently
Using take up the mantle for a physical object in everyday speech, which sounds overly formal
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is addereth, a large mantle or robe. In 1 Kings 19:13 (RSV), Elijah wraps his face in his mantle. In 2 Kings 2:8 and 2:13 (RSV), Elijah's mantle parts the Jordan, and after Elijah is taken up, the mantle falls and Elisha takes it up, a sign of inheriting the prophetic office.

mantle.etymology: From Middle English *mantel*, from Old English *mæntel*, *mentel* (“sleeveless cloak”), from **mantel*; later reinforced by Anglo-Norman *mantel*, both from Latin *mantellum* (“covering, cloak”), diminutive of *mantum*, probably from **mantos*, **mantalos*…

senses.definition: The inflorescence of the Cannabis sativa plant, smoked or ingested for euphoric effect.
senses.example: After smoking a bowl of that fine marijuana, they ate some brownies.

senses.definition: The hemp plant itself, Cannabis sativa.
senses.example: Botanists classify marijuana as Cannabis sativa, a plant with a long history of cultivation.

core.definition: The dried flowers and leaves of the cannabis plant, smoked or eaten for its mind-altering effects.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, WAH. The middle 'j' sound is an 'h' sound in American speech, so say 'wah-nuh' and not 'hoo-AH-nuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in news, law and medical settings. In casual talk it can carry a social or political charge, and friends may say 'pot' or 'weed' instead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use marijuana in the news, in law, and in everyday talk. Laws differ widely by state: many states allow adult recreational use, and many allow medical use, but it remains illegal under federal law. In medical settings, people often say cannabis, and a clinician might ask, 'Do you use cannabis?'

distinctions.note: Cannabis is the broader scientific and medical term for the plant; marijuana is the everyday name, usually for the smokable flower.
Hemp is cannabis bred for low THC content and used for fiber, seeds or oil; marijuana refers to the high-THC flower.

examples.everyday: My cousin says marijuana is legal for adults in Colorado, but he still keeps it out of the house.
examples.professional: Our benefits team asked whether the insurance plan covers medical marijuana prescriptions.
examples.analytical: The study measured how marijuana use affected reaction time among adults who completed the same driving course.

nuance.etymology: From Mexican Spanish marihuana; the origin of that word is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle as a j or hoo sound, as in 'mar-ih-HWAH-na'
Using marijuana for hemp fiber or CBD products without distinguishing them

senses.definition: Synonym of sailor, particularly one on a maritime vessel.
senses.example: The old mariner told us stories of storms he had survived at sea.

core.definition: A sailor, especially one who works on a ship at sea.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is an unstressed r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'ner,' not 'ney' or 'nee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to romantic. It sounds traditional and adventurous, often used in poetry or in stories about the sea.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use mariner in everyday talk. They say sailor or sailors. Mariner appears in literature, historical writing, maritime heritage displays, and some official or company language, such as 'merchant mariner.' Using it casually in a conversation about a fishing trip might sound overly dramatic or old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Sailor is the common everyday word for anyone who works on boats or ships, while mariner sounds more literary or traditional.
Seaman is more formal and often used for enlisted sailors or merchant crew in official contexts.
A navigator is the person who plans and directs a ship's route, which is a specific job, whereas a mariner is any sea-going worker.

examples.everyday: My grandfather was a mariner for forty years, so he has a story about every storm off the coast.
examples.professional: Merchant mariners on this vessel must complete the new safety certification before the next voyage.
examples.analytical: Coleridge's Ancient Mariner becomes a figure of guilt and redemption, and his suffering reveals the moral weight of the sea voyage.

nuance.analogy: A mariner is to the ship what a pilot is to the airplane: the skilled person whose work is tied to the vessel and its voyage.
nuance.etymology: From Old French marinier, from Latin marinarius, of the sea, from marinus.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the final syllable as 'ner' with a clear 'eh' vowel, when American speech uses a reduced r-colored vowel.
Using mariner in ordinary conversation where sailor is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture, sea-going people appear mainly in the Old Testament descriptions of trade and sea travel. The Hebrew word behind 'mariners' in Ezekiel is ḥobelim, men who handled oars, ropes, and ship rigging. In Ezekiel 27, the prophet lists the skilled mariners and pilots of the great trading city Tire, whose ships carried goods across the sea. Psalm 107:23-30 describes people who go down to the sea in ships, and how God rescues them from storms. These passages present mariners as ordinary workers whose lives depend on God's protection.

senses.definition: The condition, or quality, of being mean (any of its definitions)
A mean act.

core.definition: The quality of being unkind, spiteful, or petty, or an act that shows such a quality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, MEEN. The double n sounds like one long n, so say 'MEEN-nuss', not 'MEE-nuh-ness'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unkind or petty behavior or character, and it can be a sharp criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use meanness in everyday talk about unkind behavior, such as 'the meanness of kids on the playground'. It can also mean stinginess with money. In formal writing, 'cruelty' or 'pettiness' may be more precise. Calling someone mean is strong, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: Cruelty is intentional suffering inflicted on others, while meanness is often smaller, more petty unkindness.
Stinginess refers specifically to unwillingness to spend or share money, while meanness covers a broader range of unkind behavior.

examples.everyday: The meanness of his joke about her haircut really hurt.
examples.professional: Her manager's meanness in the performance review made the whole team afraid to speak up.
examples.analytical: Some moral theorists treat meanness of spirit as a vice that narrows one's concern for others.

nuance.analogy: Meanness is like a small thorn: it may seem minor, but it keeps hurting.
nuance.etymology: From the adjective mean (base, low), from Old English gemǣne, 'common, shared', plus -ness.
common_mistakes: Using meanness to describe only money; it can refer to any unkind behavior.
Pronouncing the double n as two separate sounds.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to the practice of medicine.
senses.example: medical doctor; medical student

senses.definition: Intended to have a therapeutic effect; medicinal.
senses.example: medical marijuana; medical cannabis; medical treatment

senses.definition: Requiring medical treatment.
senses.example: A costly medical condition can bankrupt you if it doesn't kill you first.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the state of one's health.
senses.example: medical examination; medical exemption; medical history; medical record; medical diagnosis

senses.definition: Pertaining to or requiring treatment by other than surgical means.
senses.example: medical ward

senses.definition: Pertaining to medication specifically (that is, pharmacotherapy), rather than to other aspects of medicine and surgery.
senses.example: medical oncology, radiation oncology, and surgical oncology

senses.definition: A medical examination.
senses.example: You'll have to get a medical before you apply for that job.

core.definition: Relating to the practice of medicine, to doctors, or to health treatment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the ending to a syllabic l, so it sounds like MED-ih-kl. Don't say meh-DIK-al, which is a common error.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word simply describes medicine and health care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use medical constantly in health care, insurance, and everyday talk, as in medical bills or medical leave. For an annual checkup, people say physical or checkup. Medical is not rude, but it can sound formal in casual speech. Medicinal refers to remedies rather than to doctors or treatment.

distinctions.note: Medicinal means having healing properties, as in medicinal herbs, while medical means relating to doctors and treatment.
Clinical describes care or study in a clinic or hospital setting, often involving direct patient observation, while medical is broader and covers the whole field.

examples.everyday: I had to take a few days off for a medical appointment, so I'll be late to the party.
examples.professional: Please attach the medical records to the claim before the end of the week.
examples.analytical: The essay questions whether medical definitions of illness can fully capture what a patient experiences as suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like the word legal for the law: it describes everything connected to the field, not one specific act.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin medicalis, from Latin medicus, physician, from mederi, to heal.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable, as in meh-DIK-al.
Saying medical examination for a routine checkup; Americans usually say physical or checkup.

medical.etymology: Borrowed from French *médical*, from Medieval Latin *medicālis*, from Latin *medicus*.

senses.definition: One that merges.
senses.example: The old bridge became a merger point where two shipping lanes converge.

senses.definition: The act or process of merging two or more parts into a single unit.
senses.example: Club mergers reduced the number of teams by half

senses.definition: The legal union of two or more corporations into a single entity, typically assets and liabilities being assumed by the buying party.
senses.example: The two regional banks announced a merger that will create the largest lender in the Midwest.

senses.definition: An absorption of one or more estate(s) or contract(s) into one other, all being held by the same owner; of several counts of accusation into one judgment, etc.
senses.example: Under the doctrine of merger, the lesser lease was absorbed into the owner's freehold title.

senses.definition: A type of sound change where two or more sounds merge into one.
senses.example: the cot-caught merger

core.definition: The legal combination of two or more companies into a single company, usually with one absorbing the other or both forming a new one.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, MUR. Say the final syllable as a reduced 'er' with no hard 'g' sound; the sound is /dʒɚ/, like 'juh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in business news. It can be positive or negative depending on the outcome for employees or customers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'merger' in business news, finance and law. In casual speech, people say 'they got bought' or 'they joined up with' instead. Technically, an acquisition is when one company buys another, while a merger is usually described as a combination of equals, though the distinction is often blurred in press coverage.

distinctions.note: An acquisition is when one company buys another and the target usually disappears. A merger is usually described as a joining of two firms, though legally they can be similar.
An alliance is a looser partnership where both companies stay independent. A merger creates one legal entity.

examples.everyday: Did you hear about the bank merger? My account is moving to a new name next year.
examples.professional: Legal is reviewing the merger agreement before we announce the deal to customers.
examples.analytical: The economist argues that a merger can improve efficiency while also reducing competition, which is why regulators examine both effects.

nuance.analogy: Like two rivers meeting to form one wider river: the banks and water become one body, even if some channels were once separate.
nuance.etymology: From 'merge' and the agent suffix '-er', from Latin mergere, 'to plunge'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'MER-ger' with a hard 'g' sound.
Using 'merger' for a simple partnership or joint project; in American business, it means a legal combination.
patterns: a merger between A and B

senses.definition: The act, or the result, of being merged.
senses.example: The merging of the two hospitals' records systems took eighteen months and a lot of patience.

core.definition: The process of combining two or more things, such as companies, files or code, into one.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with the 'ur' vowel. The ending is a short 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a process, sometimes with worry about job losses or change.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'merging' for the process itself, such as 'the merging of the two databases'. For a completed corporate combination, they usually say 'merger'. You also see it on highway signs, where 'merging traffic' means cars joining a lane.

distinctions.note: Merger is the completed or formal combination of companies; merging describes the ongoing process.
An acquisition is one company buying another; a merging is usually presented as two parties combining.

examples.everyday: Watch out for the car merging into our lane on the freeway.
examples.professional: The merging of the two teams is on track for next quarter.
examples.analytical: The merging of distinct traditions into a single narrative often erases the tensions that made each one meaningful.

nuance.analogy: Merging is like two rivers joining where the water mixes into one channel.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mergere 'to dip, immerse', through the verb 'merge'.
common_mistakes: Using 'merging' as the name of a finished company deal instead of 'merger'.
Confusing it with 'emerging', which means coming into view.
Saying 'merge with' versus 'merge to' carelessly; the usual pattern is 'merge with' or 'merge into'.

senses.definition: "Learning to learn": training a model so it can adapt quickly to new tasks.
senses.example: Meta-learning lets the model adapt to a new image classification task with only five examples.

core.definition: In machine learning, training a model to learn how to learn, so it can adapt quickly to new tasks using only a few examples.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on learning, with the r-colored vowel in 'learn.' Keep meta- short and unstressed, and don't say 'meet-uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical; in AI discussions it signals ambition about efficient, adaptable models.
nuance.usage_note: Among American machine learning researchers and engineers, meta-learning is a common term, often used alongside few-shot learning. Outside technical settings, Americans would just say 'learning to learn' or 'adapting quickly.' It is usually written with a hyphen in papers and talks.

distinctions.note: Transfer learning reuses knowledge from one task for another; meta-learning trains a model across many tasks so it learns how to adapt to new ones.
Few-shot learning is the goal of learning from few examples; meta-learning is one common method for achieving it.

examples.everyday: My friend who works in AI says meta-learning is basically teaching a computer how to learn quickly from very little.
examples.professional: We are testing a meta-learning approach so the recommendation model can adapt to a new market with only a few hundred users.
examples.analytical: Meta-learning reframes generalization as a property of a learning procedure across tasks, rather than of a single fixed hypothesis.

nuance.analogy: Meta-learning is like a student who has practiced so many kinds of puzzles that she can pick up the rules of a new puzzle after seeing one example.
nuance.etymology: Meta- from Greek meta, 'after' or 'beyond,' applied to learning, which comes from Old English leornian.
common_mistakes: Stressing meta- as 'MET-uh' when the main stress is on learning.
Pronouncing learning with a short vowel instead of the r-colored 'ur' sound.
Using meta-learning casually for any study skill; it is a technical machine learning term.

conversation.text: Meta-learning trains a model across many tasks so it can adapt quickly to a new task.
Our meta-learning approach adapts to a new customer with just a handful of labeled examples.

senses.definition: Any substance produced by, or taking part in, a metabolic reaction.

core.definition: A substance produced or used during metabolism, the chemical processes that keep a living body functioning.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, TAB, and the first syllable is a reduced 'ih' sound, not 'MY'. Non-native speakers often stress the final syllable or pronounce the middle vowel too clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in medicine, biology, nutrition and lab science, for example when a doctor explains blood or urine test results. In everyday talk people say 'what your body breaks a food down into' or just 'byproduct', but in a lab or clinic 'metabolite' is the standard term.

distinctions.note: Metabolism is the whole process of chemical change in a living body, while a metabolite is one specific substance produced or used in that process.
Byproduct is a general word for anything produced as a side result of a process, while metabolite refers specifically to chemicals made by metabolism.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the blood test checks for a metabolite that shows how well my body handles caffeine.
examples.professional: The lab flagged one metabolite that is elevated in the treated samples, so we need to rerun the assay before we report it.
examples.analytical: A metabolite is best understood by its place in a pathway, since its identity depends on what produced it and what consumes it.

nuance.analogy: If metabolism is the whole factory running, a metabolite is one of the intermediate parts moving along the assembly line.
nuance.etymology: From metabolism, from Greek metabolē 'change', with the suffix -ite used for chemical substances.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable as in 'metabolite' with 'LITE' at the end; the stress is on TAB.
Using 'metabolite' for the whole process; say 'metabolism' for the process itself.

senses.definition: The act of changing in form, shape, or substance; transformation by supernatural means; an instance of this.
senses.example: In the myth, the goddess's curse brought about a metamorphosis of the prince into a stag.

senses.definition: Noticeable change in character, appearance, function, or condition; an instance of this.
senses.example: After her first year as a manager, her metamorphosis from shy intern to confident leader amazed everyone.

senses.definition: Change in the form and often habits of an animal (or, in obsolete usage, a plant) after the embryonic stage during normal development (e.g. the transformation of a caterpillar into a butterfly or a tadpole into a frog); an instance of this.
senses.example: In biology class we watched a tadpole undergo metamorphosis into a frog over several weeks.

senses.definition: (rare) Change, usually degenerative, in the structure of a specific body tissue; an instance of this.
senses.example: The pathologist noted a metamorphosis of the bronchial lining in the tissue sample.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) Evolutionary change in the form of an organ; change of one type of organ into another; an instance of this.
senses.example: Some paleontologists argue that the fin underwent metamorphosis into a limb in early tetrapods.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A complete change in form, character or condition, such as a caterpillar becoming a butterfly, or a dramatic personal or institutional transformation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, -MOR-, and keep the r clearly pronounced. Reduce the middle syllables to schwa, and end with 'sis,' not 'sus.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests a striking, often dramatic, transformation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use metamorphosis in biology and in general speech about striking change, such as 'a metamorphosis of the city' or 'the company's metamorphosis.' In casual talk, people may say 'a total transformation' instead. In religious contexts, it is also used for spiritual change, which is closely linked to Romans 12:2.

distinctions.note: Transformation is the everyday word for any major change; metamorphosis suggests a complete change in form, often with biological or dramatic overtones.
Evolution refers to gradual change over generations; metamorphosis refers to a more abrupt change within one life.

examples.everyday: My little brother has gone through a metamorphosis since he started playing soccer, and now he's way more confident.
examples.professional: The company has undergone a metamorphosis from a hardware maker into a software services business over five years.
examples.analytical: In Pauline theology, the believer's inner metamorphosis is connected to the renewal of the mind rather than to moral effort alone.

nuance.analogy: A metamorphosis is like a caterpillar weaving a cocoon and emerging a butterfly: the same creature, but a completely new form.
nuance.etymology: From Greek metamorphōsis, 'a transformation,' from metamorphoein, 'to change form.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable with a strong vowel instead of a schwa.
Using metamorphosis for a small change; it implies a complete transformation.
Confusing the noun metamorphosis with the verb metamorphose in sentences.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek verb metamorphoō ('to change form or transform') is the basis for this word, though the noun metamorphosis does not appear in the New Testament. Key passages: Romans 12:2, which urges believers to be transformed by the renewal of their mind; 2 Corinthians 3:18, which speaks of being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another; and Mark 9:2, which describes Jesus being transfigured before Peter, James and John on a high mountain.
patterns: [C, U, pl. metamorphoses] a metamorphosis from A into B

metamorphosis.etymology: Latin *metamorphōsis*, from Ancient Greek *μεταμόρφωσις* (“transformation”), from *μεταμορφόω* (“to transform, disguise”) + *-σῐς*; the former is from *μετᾰ-*, + *μορφόω* (“to shape, form”).

senses.definition: The writing of computer programs that write or manipulate other programs or themselves as their data, or that perform operations at runtime that would typically be done at compile time.
senses.example: Our team used metaprogramming to generate boilerplate model classes automatically at runtime from the schema.

core.definition: Writing programs that generate, analyze or modify other programs, or that change their own behavior at runtime instead of at compile time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MEE, the first syllable, and give light secondary stress to PROH and GRAM. The -ing ending is a reduced 'ing', not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a technical term and sounds clever to some and complex to others.
nuance.usage_note: Software engineers in the United States use this word mainly when discussing code generation, macros, reflection or frameworks. It is a technical term, so it is common in code reviews and technical design docs but not in everyday talk. Explain it briefly when you use it with non-programmers.

distinctions.note: Programming writes code to perform tasks, while metaprogramming writes code that works on code itself.
Reflection lets a program inspect its own structure at runtime, which is one technique within metaprogramming.
Code generation creates new source code, which is one form of metaprogramming, but metaprogramming is the broader term.

examples.everyday: My cousin is a software developer, and she says her job is mostly writing code that writes other code, which she calls metaprogramming.
examples.professional: We used metaprogramming to generate the API client from the schema, so we don't have to maintain it by hand.
examples.analytical: The advantage of metaprogramming is that it shifts repetitive decisions from the programmer into the compiler or runtime, but it can make the resulting system harder to reason about.

nuance.analogy: Metaprogramming is like a recipe that writes other recipes: instead of cooking one meal, you write the rules that produce many dishes.
nuance.etymology: From meta- (about itself) plus programming.
common_mistakes: Using it for ordinary coding or for anything with the word 'meta' in it; it means programs that act on programs.
Mispronouncing 'meta' as 'MET-uh' when the vowel in the first syllable is long, as in 'MEE-tuh'.

senses.definition: Lasting for only a moment.
Ephemeral or relatively short-lived.
senses.example: The momentary silence after the announcement felt longer than it actually was.

core.definition: Lasting only a very short time, such as a moment, a brief pause, or a quick feeling.
